title: Embedded & IoT Engineer
tagline: Program the tiny computers inside cars, medical devices, wearables and smart homes.
about: Embedded engineers write software for microcontrollers and devices with tight limits on memory, power and timing. You'll read datasheets, talk to sensors over hardware buses, write firmware in C or Rust and debug with oscilloscopes as well as debuggers.
Start with an inexpensive development board; seeing an LED blink because of your code never gets old.
day: Write firmware in C or Rust
Bring up new hardware and drivers
Talk to sensors over I2C, SPI and UART

nodes.d: Pointers, bit manipulation, volatile and fixed-width integers.
links: CS50x: Harvard's intro to computer science

nodes.d: Voltage, current, resistance and reading a schematic.
Blink an LED, read a button, print over serial.
Configure hardware by setting bits in memory-mapped registers.
links: Nand2Tetris: build a computer from first principles

project.d: A microcontroller reading temperature and light sensors, displaying values on a small screen and logging them over serial.

phases.title: Firmware engineering
phases.goal: Write reliable firmware on real microcontrollers.

nodes.d: How chips talk to each other.
Respond to events instantly and keep precise time.
Tasks, scheduling and synchronisation with an RTOS.
Make batteries last months instead of days.

project.d: Firmware with multiple RTOS tasks (sensing, display, logging) communicating through queues, with low-power sleep between readings.

nodes.d: Wi-Fi, Bluetooth Low Energy and MQTT.
Linux on single-board computers and custom images.
Secure boot, encrypted communication and safe updates.
Unit tests on the host, hardware-in-the-loop tests.

project.d: A battery-powered device that sends sensor data over MQTT to a dashboard, supports secure over-the-air updates and runs for a week on one charge.

interview: C questions: pointers, volatile, bit manipulation.
Explain interrupts and race conditions in ISRs.
Protocol questions: I2C vs SPI vs UART.
